title: Coding the search and sort algorithms
sub: Worksheet for the 360° experience: Searching and sorting
objectives: know how to code a linear search and a binary search
understand how a bubble sort, an insertion sort and a merge sort each put a list in order
know why a binary search needs its list to be in order before it starts
starter: The sorted list holds 3, 8, 12, 19, 24, 31, 40. Write down the item a binary search looks at first, second and third while hunting for 31, and how many comparisons that took.

stations.name: Linear search
stations.fact: A linear search over a million items may need a million comparisons, which is why sorted data is worth having.
stations.challenge: Why must 'not found' be decided after the loop has finished?

stations.name: Binary search
stations.fact: Doubling the list adds only one more comparison, so a million items need about twenty.
stations.challenge: How much of the list can a binary search rule out with its first comparison?

stations.name: Bubble sort
stations.fact: A whole pass with no swaps at all means the list is already in order, so the sort can stop there.
stations.challenge: How does a bubble sort know that it can stop early?

logic.title: Tick each one off as its tests pass in the editor

rows: Ask the user for a line of whole numbers separated by single spaces. Sort them smallest first by swapping neighbouring pairs. Write the sort yourself rather than using sorted() or .sort(). Display [the sorted numbers] on one line.

stations.name: Insertion sort
stations.fact: An insertion sort is how most people sort a hand of cards without ever being taught to.
stations.challenge: Which part of the list is already sorted part way through an insertion sort?

rows: Ask the user for a line of whole numbers separated by single spaces. Sort them smallest first with an insertion sort of your own, moving each item back among the items before it. Display [the sorted numbers] on one line.

Ask the user for a line of five words separated by single spaces. Insertion sort them into alphabetical order. Write the sort yourself rather than using sorted() or .sort(). Display [the whole list] after each word from the second onwards, one list per line.

stations.name: Merge sort
stations.fact: A merge sort usually beats a bubble sort, but it needs extra memory to hold the pieces.
stations.challenge: Why is merging two sorted lists easier than sorting one unsorted one?

Ask the user for a line of whole numbers separated by single spaces. Sort them smallest first by splitting the list in half, sorting each half the same way and merging the two. Write the sort yourself rather than using sorted() or .sort(). Display [the sorted numbers] on one line.

stations.name: Putting it together
stations.fact: Sorting costs time too, so for one single search a linear search of unsorted data can still win.
stations.challenge: Plan an experiment that shows a binary search beating a linear one.

keyq: Why is a binary search so much faster than a linear search on a long list, and what does using one cost you?
exam: A linear search prints Not found from inside its loop, so searching one list prints that message several times. State where the message should go instead, and explain why putting it there fixes the problem.
Write a program that reads 8 whole numbers into a list, puts them in order using a bubble sort, and prints the sorted list.
Write a program that uses a binary search to look for a membership number the user types in, within a list of 10 numbers already in order, and prints its position or Not found.
